newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian unions exonerate self from fuel crisis.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian unions exonerate self from fuel crisis.

text.p: Oil sector unions representing employees of the state-owned Nigerian National Petroleum Corp (NNPC) said on Monday that output from the nation's refineries remained enough for local consumption and exonerated their members from Nigeria's perennial fuel supply problems.

"The authority of the NNPC ends as soon as product tankers leave our loading bays," M.K. Kyari, chairman of the white-collar Petroleum and Gas Senior Staff Association of Nigeria (PENGASSAN) in the NNPC told a news conference.
"Little wonder that diversion of products at jetties and on transit have continued to constitute a major source of disruption of supplies," he added.
Fuel scarcity gripped Nigeria in intermittent spells since the beginning of the year, reaching a peak in June when it forced economic activities to a halt.

Officials gave conflicting reasons for the situation, at times blaming smuggling of petroleum products to neighbouring countries where they fetch higher prices, malfunctioning refineries and inadequate supply of crude to the refineries.
Relief finally came in late June when military ruler General Sani Abacha ordered the importation of refined oil products.

While admitting that several components of the refineries required "total overhaul," Kyari said NNPC's four refineries could still process at 80 percent of their installed capacity of 455,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude.
He said the current daily allocation to the refineries was a mere 150,000 bpd. "There is a staggering shortfall of 200,000 barrels a day," he added.

A joint statement signed by Kyari and his counterpart of the blue-collar National Union of Petroleum and Gas Workers (NUPENG) Ben Awe called on the government to fund the industry properly for optimum performance.

"Our conclusion is that some interest groups desire the grounding of the national oil corporation in order that the future of our nation be mortgaged," said the statement, an oblique reference to calls for privatisation of the oil sector.

While the unions want the government to properly identify the problems of the refineries in order to solve them, they also do not want a situation where they say the government will be forced to sell the refineries to foreginers and end subsidies.
"Considering the level of poverty in this country, I think it is reasonable that people get this subsidy, but the current price of 11 naira a litre is not sustainable," said Kyari.
